title: Spotting third-law pairs
canonical_question: How can you spot which two forces form a Newton third-law pair?
summary: To spot a third-law pair, find the two objects that touch or interact and describe the force each exerts on the other.
In a collision between a bat and a ball, the bat exerts a force on the ball and the ball exerts an equal and opposite force on the bat.

reuse.rationale: Authored fixture node for the E05 registry.

sections.heading: The two-body test
sections.body_md: To spot a third-law pair, find the two objects that touch or interact and describe the force each exerts on the other. The pair is those two forces: same magnitude, opposite direction, one on each body. Anything acting on just one object is disqualified.

sections.heading: Collision example
sections.body_md: In a collision between a bat and a ball, the bat exerts a force on the ball and the ball exerts an equal and opposite force on the bat. Those two forces are the pair even though the ball flies off and the bat barely moves. Different masses, same paired forces.

key_points: Pairs act on two different bodies.
Unequal motion does not mean unequal forces.
core.bridge_to_parent: It gives a second route to the objective’s pair identification.

seeds: If forces are equal, why do outcomes differ?
